{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"b271b95efc0e1901017642e89662473796b49e6654dc4c7fb146cb2397f661d1","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:103","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Interstate driving","heading":"C — Interstate driving: trip preparation, entering and merging, lane use, following distance, speed and traffic flow, HOV lanes, exiting, interchanges, prohibited moves, interstate hypnosis, the Move Over Law and breakdowns","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Interstate driving: trip preparation, entering and merging, lane use, following distance, speed and traffic flow, HOV lanes, exiting, interchanges, prohibited moves, interstate hypnosis, the Move Over Law and breakdowns
Knowledge domain: how to drive on Tennessee interstates — why controlled access makes them different, how to prepare, enter and merge, which lane to use and how far to follow, how to keep pace legally, the HOV lane rules, how to exit, how diamond, cloverleaf and weaving interchanges work, what is forbidden on an interstate, how to fight highway hypnosis, the Move Over Law, and what to do after a breakdown or crash.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
Interstates are controlled-access roads with no stop signs, railroad crossings or traffic lights, and drivers get on and off only at interchanges without crossing other traffic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
Plan your entrance, direction and exit ahead of time, and check your fuel first, since rural exits can be many miles apart. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
If you cannot or do not want to drive at least the minimum speed, do not use the interstate. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
Unlike entering most busy roads, entering an interstate means speeding up: use the acceleration lane to reach traffic speed, signal left and merge when the way is clear. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
The entering driver must yield the right-of-way to vehicles already on the interstate. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
Do not stop at the end of an on-ramp; if you must wait for a gap, slow down on the ramp so you still have room to build speed, because stopping invites rear-end crashes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
A lane added sign means the ramp becomes a new lane so entering traffic need not merge at once, and through drivers should avoid moving right there. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A01
A merge sign means traffic from the right must merge into the existing right lane, so drivers already on the interstate should watch for it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A01
On multi-lane interstates, leave the far left lane for faster traffic, and do not ride alongside other vehicles where you sit in their blind spots. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
Move to the right lane early when you plan to exit, to avoid last-second lane changes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
On the interstate stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead, and at least four seconds in bad weather, at night and on higher-speed rural stretches. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
Scan about 15 to 20 seconds ahead for vehicles braking, entering or leaving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
If traffic ahead slows or stops, tap your brake pedal lightly several times to warn the drivers behind you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
Keep pace with traffic but never exceed the posted limit to stay with the flow, and if you drive slower than the flow, use the right lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
Driving too slowly on an interstate is illegal because it is as dangerous as speeding. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A02
The left lane is for passing only; if a faster driver comes up behind you there, move one lane to the right. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A02
During the morning peak of 7 to 9 a.m. and the evening peak of 4 to 6 p.m., the HOV lane is reserved for vehicles with two or more people, motorcycles, buses and emergency vehicles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A02
A baby in a car seat counts as a passenger for the HOV lane, and a single driver may not use it during peak hours even to pass. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A02
Outside peak weekday hours and on weekends, the HOV lane works as an ordinary lane, and an HOV violation brings a $50 fine plus court costs. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A02
Exit signs usually appear at least one mile before the exit, and in heavier traffic you should get into the exit lane sooner. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A02
Keep your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the ramp's posted speed and on to the limit of the road you are joining [A02] [A03].
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
Do not drive on the interstate's paved shoulder except where marked for slowing down or in an emergency. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A03
Parking on any part of an entrance or exit ramp is illegal unless the vehicle is disabled. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A03
Backing up, making a U-turn or crossing the median on an interstate is illegal; if you miss your exit, go on to the next one. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A03
At a diamond interchange the exit ramp always comes before you pass over or under the cross road, and you then obey its sign or signal and turn as at any intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A03
From the cross road at a diamond interchange, the right-turn entrance ramp comes before you cross the interstate and the left-turn ramp after it, never the other way around. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A03
At a cloverleaf interchange every turn is a right turn: to go left, take the right-hand ramp just after the overpass. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A03
A weaving interchange, where entering and exiting traffic share one lane, is among the most hazardous spots and calls for give-and-take from every driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A04
On the interstate you may not change lanes without signaling, drive in another driver's blind spot, or get on except through a provided entrance. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A04
Night driving is far more dangerous per mile than daytime driving, mainly because of fatigue and poor vision, and drinking drivers are more often out at night. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A04
Interstate hypnosis is drowsiness or unawareness brought on by long monotonous driving and the steady sound of wind, engine and tires. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A04
To fight interstate hypnosis, keep your eyes moving, keep the car cool, and stop as soon as you feel drowsy, since drowsiness is the first step to falling asleep. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A04
Stop and step out of the car for a rest at least every two hours or about every 100 miles, and avoid driving more than eight hours a day. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A05
Rubbernecking, tailgating, needless lane changes and inattention all cause crashes and add to congestion. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A05
The Move Over Law requires you to leave an empty lane next to a stopped emergency, utility, maintenance or recovery vehicle with flashing lights on an interstate or other highway with two or more lanes your way. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A05
Moving over applies whichever shoulder the vehicle is on, and you may simply slow down in your lane only when a lane change would be unsafe. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A05
The Move Over rule also covers any stopped vehicle on the shoulder, emergency lane or median that is showing flashing lights, including ordinary cars and trucks. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A05
With car trouble, get onto the right shoulder or an emergency stopping area quickly and switch on your flashers. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec10-F39 | anchor: A06
After an interstate crash with no serious injuries or deaths, Tennessee law lets you move a drivable vehicle to the emergency lane to wait for police. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec10-F40 | anchor: A06
Never move a seriously injured person unless emergency personnel tell you to, never disturb a fatal crash scene, and never leave the scene of any crash. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec10-F41 | anchor: A06
Dial *THP, which is *847, from a cell phone at no charge to reach the nearest Tennessee Highway Patrol dispatcher in an emergency or to report a dangerous driver. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0087]

Misconceptions: you speed up, not slow down, to enter an interstate; stopping at the end of an on-ramp is dangerous, not cautious; a lane added sign is not a merge sign; slowing in your lane satisfies the Move Over Law only when changing lanes is unsafe; a missed exit never justifies backing up or using a crossover.
Mnemonics: speed up to merge; two seconds, four when it is dark, wet or fast; every two hours or a hundred miles, take a break; *THP for the Highway Patrol.
Glossary: interchange means a set of ramps connecting an interstate with another road; acceleration lane means the ramp lane used to reach interstate speed; deceleration lane means the exit lane used to slow down; interstate hypnosis means drowsiness caused by long monotonous driving.
Dynamic facts: HOV hours and fines, the *THP service, HELP truck coverage and the Move Over Law details can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
